questions.subdomain: 1.1 Implement metrics, alarms, and filters by using AWS monitoring and logging services.
questions.question: When one backend dependency fails, five CloudWatch metric alarms fire and on-call engineers are paged five times for one incident. The team wants a single page, sent only when the high-latency alarm and the high-error-rate alarm are both in ALARM state. What should the CloudOps engineer configure?
options: Increase the number of evaluation periods on each of the five metric alarms
A shared CloudWatch dashboard that displays the five alarms side by side
A composite alarm that requires both alarms to be in ALARM, with the alert action set on it
An EventBridge rule that forwards each state change from the five alarms to one SNS topic
questions.correct_rationale: A composite alarm evaluates the states of other alarms. Its rule can require that all referenced alarms are in ALARM, and AWS describes setting up alerts only for the composite alarm to reduce alarm noise.
distractor_rationales: More evaluation periods delays each alarm but still produces five separate notifications per incident.
A dashboard helps people see the alarms together, but it does not change who gets paged or how often.
Forwarding every state change to one topic still delivers five messages, and it ignores the AND condition.
questions.distractor_summary: Each distractor changes timing, display or routing; only a composite alarm adds the AND logic and a single alert.

questions.question: A CloudOps engineer must alarm on memory utilization and disk usage inside the operating system of a fleet of EC2 instances. The metrics that EC2 publishes to CloudWatch by default do not include this in-guest data. What should the engineer do?
options: Install and configure the CloudWatch agent on the instances to collect in-guest metrics
Turn on AWS CloudTrail data events for the account so that each instance is recorded
Create VPC flow logs for the instances' subnets and a metric filter on the log group
Enable Amazon EC2 automatic recovery on each instance and alarm on the resulting recovery events
questions.correct_rationale: The CloudWatch agent collects internal system-level metrics from EC2 instances, including in-guest metrics, in addition to the standard EC2 metrics. Alarms can then use those metrics.
distractor_rationales: CloudTrail records actions taken through the console, CLI, SDKs and APIs. It does not collect operating system metrics.
Flow logs capture information about IP traffic to and from network interfaces, not memory or disk usage.
Automatic recovery acts when a system status check fails. It does not publish memory or disk metrics.
questions.distractor_summary: CloudTrail, flow logs and recovery each observe something else; only the agent reads inside the guest OS.

questions.question: AWS Config rules already flag noncompliant resources in an account. The security lead wants noncompliant resources fixed by a managed AWS mechanism tied to those rules, without the team building and running its own polling script. What should the CloudOps engineer configure?
options: A CloudFormation StackSet that redeploys every flagged resource each night
An AWS CloudTrail trail that reverts each change recorded in Event history
A CloudWatch composite alarm with an EC2 action that runs on each finding
Remediation actions on the Config rules that use Systems Manager Automation documents
questions.correct_rationale: AWS Config remediates noncompliant resources by using Systems Manager Automation documents associated with the rules. Config provides managed automation documents, and you can also create custom ones.
distractor_rationales: StackSets create, update or delete stacks across accounts and Regions. They do not act on Config rule evaluations, and a nightly redeploy is a blunt tool.
CloudTrail records events, and Event history is a searchable record of management events. It does not undo changes.
Composite alarms evaluate alarm states and cannot perform EC2 actions. They are not linked to Config findings.
questions.distractor_summary: The distractors deploy, record or alarm; only Config remediation with Automation documents fixes flagged resources.

questions.question: A database runs on a 200 GiB gp2 volume. CloudWatch shows the volume repeatedly running out of burst credits, and the workload needs a steady 6,000 IOPS. The team does not need more storage and does not want to pay for extra capacity only to raise performance. What should the CloudOps engineer do?
options: Grow the gp2 volume until its size-based baseline IOPS reaches the required level
Modify the volume type to gp3 and provision 6,000 IOPS at the current size
Move the database files to an instance store volume on a larger instance type
Snapshot the volume and restore it to a new gp2 volume of equal size
questions.correct_rationale: gp3 lets you scale performance independently of volume size, and gp3 does not use burst credits. A 200 GiB gp3 volume can be provisioned above its 3,000 IOPS baseline (up to 500 IOPS per GiB) without adding capacity.
distractor_rationales: Growing gp2 raises IOPS only by adding capacity, which is the cost the team wants to avoid.
Instance store data is temporary and is lost when the instance stops, which is unsafe for database files.
A new gp2 volume of the same size has the same baseline and the same burst behavior.
questions.distractor_summary: Bigger gp2, same-size gp2 and instance store all miss the goal; gp3 decouples IOPS from size.

questions.question: A Lambda-based API opens a new database connection on each invocation. During traffic spikes, the RDS for MySQL instance shows high CPU and memory from connection churn, and some new connections are refused. Read and write traffic are both affected. The team wants a fix with minimal code changes. What should the CloudOps engineer do?
options: Add a read replica and point the Lambda function at the replica endpoint
Raise the Lambda function's memory so each invocation can open connections faster
Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance and use the proxy endpoint
Change the DB instance storage to gp3 and provision more IOPS and throughput
questions.correct_rationale: RDS Proxy keeps a pool of database connections and reuses them, which avoids the memory and CPU overhead of opening a new connection each time. Most applications can use it with no code changes beyond the endpoint.
distractor_rationales: A read replica is read-only, so writes cannot move to it, and each invocation would still open new connections.
More function memory does not reduce how many new database connections are opened.
Storage IOPS do not address the CPU and memory cost of opening connections.
questions.distractor_summary: Replicas, function memory and storage miss the cause; pooling connections with RDS Proxy addresses the churn.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement scalability and elasticity.
questions.question: An Auto Scaling group uses step scaling with three CloudWatch alarms that engineers tune by hand. The team wants the group to hold average CPU utilization near 50 percent and wants AWS to create and manage the alarms. What should the CloudOps engineer configure?
options: A target tracking policy on average CPU utilization with a target value of 50
A step scaling policy with more step adjustments for each size of alarm breach
A CloudWatch composite alarm that combines the three alarms into one scaling trigger
A simple scaling policy with a longer cooldown period between scaling activities
questions.correct_rationale: With target tracking you select a metric and a target value, and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms. AWS strongly recommends target tracking for metrics such as average CPU utilization.
distractor_rationales: With step scaling you still create and manage the CloudWatch alarms yourself.
Composite alarms cannot perform Auto Scaling actions.
Simple scaling also relies on alarms you manage, and a cooldown only spaces out scaling activities.
questions.distractor_summary: Step, simple and composite options all leave alarm management with the team; target tracking hands it to AWS.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement scalability and elasticity.
questions.question: Business reporting queries slow down an RDS for PostgreSQL production instance during working hours. The reports can tolerate data that is slightly behind production. Which change offloads this load with the least impact on the application's writes?
options: Put RDS Proxy in front of the instance and connect the reporting tool through it
Increase the backup retention period so that reports can read from automated backups
Create an AWS Backup plan that takes snapshots of the instance every hour
Create a read replica and point the reporting tool at the replica's endpoint
questions.correct_rationale: AWS lists running business reporting queries against a read replica, rather than the production instance, as a read replica use case. Replication is asynchronous, which is acceptable because the reports tolerate slightly stale data.
distractor_rationales: RDS Proxy pools connections, but the reporting queries would still run on the production instance.
Automated backups support restores. They are not a queryable endpoint for reports.
Snapshots protect data. Querying them would first require restoring to a new instance each time.
questions.distractor_summary: Proxy, retention and snapshots leave queries on production or need restores; a replica serves reads directly.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement highly available and resilient environments.
questions.question: New EC2 targets registered in an Application Load Balancer target group stay unhealthy. The application answers correctly when tested from inside each instance. The health check uses HTTP on port 8080. Which configuration issue explains this behavior?
options: The instances lack an IAM role that lets them report health to Elastic Load Balancing
The instance security group does not allow port 8080 from the load balancer
The target group has no registered targets, so the load balancer returns HTTP 503
The Auto Scaling group uses target tracking instead of a step scaling policy
questions.correct_rationale: The security group associated with an instance must allow traffic from the load balancer on the health check port and protocol. If it does not, health checks fail even though the application works locally.
distractor_rationales: The load balancer sends health check requests to the targets. Targets do not need a role to report their health.
The scenario states that targets are registered. HTTP 503 with no registered targets is a different symptom.
The scaling policy type controls capacity changes. It does not affect whether health checks reach the targets.
questions.distractor_summary: Only the security group blocks the health check path; the other options describe unrelated settings or symptoms.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement highly available and resilient environments.
questions.question: A company hosts its website in one Region and keeps a static maintenance page in an S3 bucket configured as a website. DNS must send users to the maintenance page only when the primary site is unhealthy, without anyone taking manual action. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Route user traffic through a CloudFront distribution whose single origin is the S3 bucket
An AWS Backup plan that copies the website content to the S3 bucket every hour
Route 53 failover routing with a health check on the primary and the bucket as secondary
A CloudWatch alarm on the site that emails the on-call engineer through an SNS topic
questions.correct_rationale: Failover routing sends traffic to a resource when it is healthy and to a different resource when the first is unhealthy. The secondary record can point to an S3 bucket set up as a website, and Route 53 health checks decide which is healthy.
distractor_rationales: A distribution with the bucket as its single origin would serve the maintenance page all the time.
Copying content to the bucket does not change where DNS sends users.
An email alert requires a person to act, which the requirement rules out.
questions.distractor_summary: CloudFront-only, backups and email alerts do not switch DNS on health; failover routing does.

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Implement backup and restore strategies.
questions.question: Teams back up EC2, EBS, RDS and DynamoDB resources with their own scripts. The company now needs one schedule, a copy of each backup in a second Region, and a single place where auditors can review backup policies. What should the CloudOps engineer implement?
options: AWS Backup plans assigned to the resources, with cross-Region copy in the plan
An S3 Lifecycle configuration that transitions the backup files to a colder storage class
Separate Systems Manager Automation runbooks for each service, run on a schedule
CloudFormation StackSets that deploy each team's backup scripts into a second Region
questions.correct_rationale: AWS Backup centrally manages backup policies, called backup plans, across AWS services. Backups can be copied to other Regions automatically as part of a scheduled backup plan.
distractor_rationales: S3 Lifecycle manages objects in S3 buckets. It does not back up EC2, RDS or DynamoDB resources.
Per-service runbooks keep custom logic in many places and give auditors no single backup policy.
Deploying the same scripts to more Regions multiplies the scripts. It does not centralize policy.
questions.distractor_summary: Lifecycle, runbooks and StackSets keep backups scattered; AWS Backup plans centralize schedule, copy and audit.

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Implement backup and restore strategies.
questions.question: At 14:20 a faulty deployment deleted rows in an RDS for MySQL production database that has automated backups enabled. The team needs the data as it existed at 14:15 and must leave the current instance untouched while it investigates. What should the CloudOps engineer do?
options: Promote the existing read replica to a standalone instance and copy the rows back
Restore to 14:15 as a new DB instance, then copy the rows back
Restore last night's automated snapshot over the production instance in place
Roll the production instance back in place to 14:15 by using its latest restorable time
questions.correct_rationale: Point-in-time restore creates a new DB instance at the chosen time without modifying the source instance. RDS uploads transaction logs every five minutes, so 14:15 is within the restorable window here.
distractor_rationales: RDS updates the replica whenever the primary changes, so the replica has already applied the deletes as well.
Last night's snapshot loses the day's legitimate changes, and the plan overwrites the instance the team must keep.
A point-in-time restore does not modify the source instance in place; it creates a new instance.
questions.distractor_summary: The replica copied the deletes and the other two touch production; point-in-time restore to a new instance fits.

questions.question: A platform team must deploy one CloudFormation template, which creates an IAM role and an SNS topic, into 40 member accounts across three Regions. Future template updates must roll out in a single operation from an administrator account. What should the team use?
options: AWS RAM to share the stack from the administrator account with each member account
A Systems Manager maintenance window that runs a Patch Manager task in each account
Separate stacks that each account team creates and updates by hand from the template
CloudFormation StackSets that target the 40 accounts and the three Regions

distractor_rationales: AWS RAM makes an existing resource usable by other accounts. It does not create stacks in them.
Patch Manager applies operating system patches to managed nodes. It does not deploy templates.
Manual per-account stacks fail the single-operation requirement and invite drift between accounts.
questions.distractor_summary: RAM shares, Patch Manager patches and manual stacks do not scale; StackSets deploy across accounts and Regions at once.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Provision and maintain cloud resources.
questions.question: A networking account owns a central VPC. Application teams in other accounts of the same organization must launch EC2 instances into its subnets without creating VPCs of their own, and the network team must keep control of routing. What should the network team do?

Deploy a StackSet that builds a copy of the central VPC in every application account
Share the subnets with the application accounts by using AWS Resource Access Manager
Create gateway VPC endpoints in the central VPC for each of the application accounts

Copying the VPC into every account removes central control and creates many separate networks.
Gateway endpoints provide private access to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. They do not let other accounts launch into subnets.
questions.distractor_summary: Peering and copies create more VPCs and endpoints do something else; RAM subnet sharing keeps one central VPC.

Copying the current AMI spreads the same unpatched image to more Regions.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Automate the management of existing resources.
questions.question: An EventBridge rule matches EC2 instance state-change events, and its metrics confirm that the rule is matching. The rule's target Lambda function is never invoked. No IAM execution role is configured on the target. What should the CloudOps engineer check first?
options: Test the rule's event pattern against sample events in the EventBridge Sandbox
Whether the function's resource-based policy allows EventBridge to invoke it
Increase the Lambda function's timeout and memory so that it can finish running
Whether the function is subscribed to the SNS topic that EventBridge publishes to
questions.correct_rationale: For Lambda targets with no IAM execution role, EventBridge relies on the resource-based policy on the function. AWS lists missing permissions as a reason a matched rule does not invoke a Lambda function.
distractor_rationales: The metrics already show the pattern matches, so testing the pattern does not explain the missing invocation.
The function is never invoked, so its timeout and memory never come into play.
EventBridge invokes Lambda targets directly. No SNS subscription is involved.
questions.distractor_summary: The pattern works and runtime settings never apply; the missing piece is permission to invoke the function.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Automate the management of existing resources.
questions.question: Each new object in an S3 bucket must be processed by consumers that read from an existing SQS FIFO queue. When the team adds the FIFO queue as the destination of an S3 event notification, the configuration is rejected. What should the CloudOps engineer do?
options: Update the FIFO queue's access policy so that the S3 service principal can send messages
Recreate the queue as a standard queue with the same name and point the consumers at it
Turn on S3 Versioning for the bucket so that each new object write produces an event
Enable Amazon EventBridge for the bucket and add a rule that targets the FIFO queue
questions.correct_rationale: SQS FIFO queues are not supported as S3 event notification destinations. AWS directs you to use Amazon EventBridge to send S3 events to an SQS FIFO queue.
distractor_rationales: The rejection is about the destination type, so changing the queue policy does not make a FIFO queue supported.
This abandons the FIFO queue that the existing consumers read from, which the requirement keeps.
Versioning keeps object versions. It does not change which destinations event notifications support.
questions.distractor_summary: Permissions, queue swaps and versioning do not lift the destination limit; EventBridge routes S3 events to FIFO.

questions.subdomain: 4.1 Implement and manage security and compliance tools and policies.
questions.question: An SCP attached at the organization root denies ec2:TerminateInstances. An administrator in the management account can still terminate instances. A developer in a member account who has the AdministratorAccess policy cannot. Which statement explains both results?
options: The SCP is still propagating and will reach the management account's users within a few hours
Permissions boundaries in the management account take priority over every SCP
SCPs skip the management account, and in member accounts they cap even full IAM rights
SCPs grant permissions in the management account and deny them in member accounts
questions.correct_rationale: SCPs do not affect users or roles in the management account. In member accounts, an SCP sets the maximum available permissions, so its deny applies even when an identity policy allows everything.
distractor_rationales: Propagation is not the cause. SCPs do not apply to the management account at all.
Permissions boundaries are not why the management account is unaffected; SCPs simply exclude it.
SCPs never grant permissions anywhere. They only set limits.
questions.distractor_summary: Timing, boundaries and grants are all wrong mechanisms; SCPs exclude the management account and cap member accounts.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Implement strategies to protect data and infrastructure.
questions.question: A CloudOps engineer must share an encrypted EBS snapshot with a partner's AWS account. The snapshot is encrypted with the default AWS managed key, and sharing fails. Which requirement must be met for the partner to use a shared encrypted snapshot?
options: Make the snapshot public first, and then let the partner account copy it
The snapshot must use a customer managed key that is also shared with the partner
Enable block public access for EBS snapshots, and then retry the private share
Share the default AWS managed key with the partner account, and keep the snapshot as it is
questions.correct_rationale: Snapshots encrypted with the default AWS managed key cannot be shared. Only snapshots encrypted with a customer managed key can be shared, and that key must be shared with the other account too.
distractor_rationales: Only unencrypted snapshots can be shared publicly, and public sharing would expose the data to everyone.
Block public access prevents public sharing. It does not make an AWS managed key snapshot shareable.
Snapshots encrypted with the default AWS managed key can't be shared, so the snapshot itself must change.
questions.distractor_summary: Public sharing, block public access and the AWS managed key all fail; a shared customer managed key is required.

questions.subdomain: 4.2 Implement strategies to protect data and infrastructure.
questions.question: An application reads RDS database credentials from a configuration file on each server. Security requires removing the hard-coded credentials and replacing them on a regular schedule without redeploying the servers. What should the CloudOps engineer implement?
options: Encrypt the configuration file with a KMS key, and rotate that key every year
Store the credentials in a versioned S3 bucket that the servers read at boot
Bake the credentials into the golden AMI that EC2 Image Builder produces
Secrets Manager with automatic rotation, retrieved by the application at runtime
questions.correct_rationale: Secrets Manager replaces hard-coded credentials with runtime retrieval, and an automatic rotation schedule replaces long-term secrets with short-term ones.
distractor_rationales: Encrypting the file keeps a long-term password in place. Rotating the encryption key does not change the database password.
A bucket still stores a static password, and nothing rotates it in the database.
Baking credentials into an image hard-codes them again and requires a rebuild to change them.
questions.distractor_summary: Encrypted files, buckets and images all keep static passwords; Secrets Manager retrieves and rotates them.

questions.subdomain: 5.1 Implement and optimize networking features and connectivity.
questions.question: EC2 instances in private subnets copy several terabytes a day to S3 buckets in the same Region through a NAT gateway, and NAT data processing charges are high. Which change reduces this cost the most while the instances stay private?
options: Move the instances to public subnets and assign each instance a public IPv4 address
Create an interface VPC endpoint for S3 in each Availability Zone used by the instances
Add a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 to the route tables of the private subnets
Replace the NAT gateway with a route to an internet gateway in the private subnets' route tables
questions.correct_rationale: A gateway endpoint gives private access to S3 without an internet gateway or NAT device, and there is no additional charge for gateway endpoints. Adding it to the subnet route tables sends S3 traffic past the NAT gateway.
distractor_rationales: Public subnets with public addresses break the requirement that the instances stay private.
An interface endpoint also avoids the NAT gateway, but it carries an additional cost that a gateway endpoint does not.
A route to an internet gateway makes the subnets public, which breaks the requirement, and instances without public addresses still could not use it.
questions.distractor_summary: Public addressing and internet gateway routes break privacy and interface endpoints cost more; the gateway endpoint is free.

A gateway VPC endpoint attached to the route tables of the instances' subnets

Global Accelerator brings inbound user traffic to endpoints, which is the opposite of the requirement.

questions.question: A custom network ACL on a public subnet allows inbound TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, and its only outbound rule allows TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0. The web server's security group allows inbound 443. Client HTTPS connections to the server time out. What change fixes the issue?

Add an outbound security group rule that allows TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0 for the server
Add a second inbound network ACL rule that allows TCP 443 with a lower rule number
Add an inbound security group rule that allows the clients' ephemeral source ports

Inbound 443 is already allowed. A duplicate inbound rule does not touch the blocked responses.
Requests arrive on port 443, which the security group already allows, and a stateful security group does not affect the NACL that drops the responses.

questions.question: Each night, a company must copy new and changed files from an on-premises NFS share to an S3 bucket. The operations team wants the transfers to run on a recurring schedule without writing or maintaining scripts. Which solution meets this need?
options: An AWS DataSync task between the NFS and S3 locations, with a task schedule
S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket, with uploads started from the file server
A cron job on the file server that runs a multipart upload script every night
An S3 Lifecycle rule on the bucket that transitions the new files every night
questions.correct_rationale: A DataSync task moves data between storage locations such as an NFS share and an S3 bucket, and a task schedule runs it periodically, so no scripts are needed.
distractor_rationales: Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads, but something still has to start and manage them on a schedule.
A cron job with a script works, but it is exactly the scripting the team wants to avoid.
Lifecycle rules act on objects already in the bucket; they do not copy files from on premises.
questions.distractor_summary: A scheduled DataSync task is the managed, script-free transfer; the others need scripts or do not copy data.

questions.question: Linux application servers mount a file share over NFS, and Windows users open the same files over SMB. The shared file system must keep serving clients if one Availability Zone fails. Which storage option meets these needs with one file system?
options: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with a Single-AZ deployment
An Amazon EFS Regional file system shared by the client instances
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with a Multi-AZ deployment
An EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach shared by every server
questions.correct_rationale: FSx for NetApp ONTAP serves the same data over NFS and SMB (and iSCSI and NVMe), and it offers Multi-AZ and Single-AZ deployment options. A Multi-AZ deployment keeps the file system available if one zone fails.
distractor_rationales: A Single-AZ deployment serves both protocols but is not built to keep serving through the loss of its zone.
EFS is accessed over NFS; Windows users opening files over SMB are not served by it.
Multi-Attach shares a block volume inside one zone and is not an NFS or SMB file share.
questions.distractor_summary: One file system for NFS and SMB that survives a zone failure is ONTAP Multi-AZ; the others miss a protocol or the zone requirement.

questions.question: An EFS file system has a lifecycle policy that moves files to Infrequent Access after 30 days without access. Some old project files have become active again and are now read many times a day, but they are still being served from Infrequent Access. What should the operations team change?
options: Shorten the transition to Infrequent Access from 30 days to 7 days
Switch the file system to Provisioned Throughput mode for the busy period
Copy the active files to a new file system created for the project
Add a lifecycle setting that moves files back to Standard on their first access
questions.correct_rationale: By default, EFS does not move files back to the Standard storage class after they transition. A lifecycle setting that transitions files into Standard on first access moves the active files back automatically.
distractor_rationales: A shorter transition moves files to Infrequent Access sooner; it does not bring active files back.
Throughput mode changes throughput, not the storage class the files sit in.
Copying files works once but adds a second file system and does not fix the policy for later files.
questions.distractor_summary: Files stay in Infrequent Access unless a transition back to Standard on first access is set.

docLinks.title: Managing storage lifecycle - Amazon Elastic File System

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement scalability and elasticity.
questions.question: An application uses lazy loading with Amazon ElastiCache in front of its database. Users sometimes see product prices that were updated in the database minutes earlier. The team wants cached prices to reflect every database update as soon as the update is written. Which caching strategy should the team adopt?
options: Write-through, updating the cache whenever the application writes to the database
Lazy loading with a longer TTL, so that cached prices expire less often
Read replicas for the cache, so that reads spread across more nodes
A larger node type, so that more prices fit in the cache at once
questions.correct_rationale: With write-through, data is added to or updated in the cache whenever it is written to the database, so cached prices match each update. Lazy loading writes to the cache only on a miss, which is why prices can be stale.
distractor_rationales: A longer TTL keeps stale prices in the cache even longer.
Read replicas spread read load; they copy whatever the primary holds, including stale prices.
More memory holds more items but does not refresh them when the database changes.
questions.distractor_summary: Staleness comes from updating the cache only on misses; write-through updates it on every write.

docLinks.title: Caching strategies for Memcached - Amazon ElastiCache

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement scalability and elasticity.
questions.question: A provisioned-mode DynamoDB table has plenty of unused write capacity, yet writes to it are throttled during a nightly import. The table has one global secondary index, and its metrics show that index consuming all of its provisioned write capacity. What is the most likely fix?
options: Raise the provisioned write capacity of the global secondary index
Raise the provisioned write capacity of the base table, leaving the index as it is
Turn on point-in-time recovery for the table before the import
Add a local secondary index that uses the same key attributes
questions.correct_rationale: When a table takes heavy writes but one of its global secondary indexes has too little write capacity, writes to the table itself are throttled. Raising the index's write capacity removes the bottleneck.
distractor_rationales: The table already has unused capacity; the index is what is starved.
Point-in-time recovery adds backups and does nothing for write capacity.
Another index adds more writes to maintain and leaves the starved index unchanged.
questions.distractor_summary: A starved global secondary index throttles writes to its base table, so the index needs capacity.

docLinks.title: Using Global Secondary Indexes in DynamoDB - Amazon DynamoDB

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement scalability and elasticity.
questions.question: A stateless batch fleet runs in one Auto Scaling group of On-Demand Instances. The team wants to keep a base of On-Demand capacity and run the rest on Spot Instances in the same group, choosing the Spot pools that are least likely to be interrupted. Which configuration meets this need?
options: A mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base and the lowest-price Spot strategy
A second Auto Scaling group of Spot Instances using the same launch template
Scheduled scaling that switches the whole group to Spot Instances at night
A mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base and the price-capacity-optimized Spot strategy
questions.correct_rationale: A mixed instances policy runs On-Demand and Spot Instances in one Auto Scaling group. The price-capacity-optimized strategy considers both price and capacity and picks the Spot pools least likely to be interrupted.
distractor_rationales: The lowest-price strategy picks pools by price alone, not by how likely they are to be interrupted.
A second group splits the fleet across two groups instead of one.
Scheduled scaling changes capacity at set times; it does not mix purchase options or choose Spot pools.
questions.distractor_summary: One group with an On-Demand base and Spot chosen by price and capacity is the mixed policy with price-capacity-optimized.

docLinks.title: Setup overview for creating a mixed instances group - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Implement scalability and elasticity.
questions.question: A reporting dashboard's read queries are overloading an RDS for MySQL DB instance, and those reads must be moved off the primary instance. Separately, bursts of Lambda invocations open thousands of short-lived connections, and those connections must be pooled and shared instead of each opening its own database connection. Which change meets both needs?
options: A read replica for the dashboard, with Lambda connecting directly to the primary
An RDS Proxy for the Lambda functions, with the dashboard reading from the primary
A Multi-AZ standby, with the dashboard and Lambda both using the primary
A read replica for the dashboard, plus an RDS Proxy for the Lambda functions
questions.correct_rationale: RDS Proxy lets applications pool and share database connections, which absorbs bursts of short-lived Lambda connections. A read replica is a read-only copy that the dashboard can query, taking that load off the primary.
distractor_rationales: The replica takes the dashboard's reads, but Lambda still opens its own connections to the primary.
The proxy pools Lambda connections, but the dashboard still loads the primary.
A standby in a Multi-AZ instance deployment does not serve reads, and nothing pools the connections.
questions.distractor_summary: Offloading reads needs a replica and pooling needs a proxy; each simpler change handles one.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement highly available and resilient environments.
questions.question: A web application runs on an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. An instance must be treated as unhealthy whenever its /health page does not return HTTP 200, even if the default path still responds. Unhealthy instances must also be terminated and replaced automatically, not just removed from rotation. Which configuration meets both needs?
options: Set the target group health check to /health with a 200 matcher, and leave the group on EC2 status health checks
Keep the default target group health check path, and turn on ELB health checks for the group
Set the target group health check to /health with a 200 matcher, and turn on ELB health checks for the group
Keep the default target group health check path, and leave the group on EC2 status health checks
questions.correct_rationale: The target group's health check path and success codes decide when the load balancer marks a target unhealthy. Elastic Load Balancing is one of the health sources Auto Scaling can use, and when the group sees an instance as unhealthy it replaces it.
distractor_rationales: The load balancer stops routing to the instance, but with EC2 checks alone the group does not replace it.
The group replaces instances the load balancer reports, but the default path does not test /health.
Neither the /health test nor automatic replacement is in place.
questions.distractor_summary: Testing /health needs the target group check and replacement needs ELB health checks on the group; each simpler setup drops one.

docLinks.title: Health checks for Application Load Balancer target groups - Elastic Load Balancing
Health checks for instances in an Auto Scaling group - Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement highly available and resilient environments.
questions.question: An application runs behind a load balancer across three Availability Zones. The operations team wants traffic moved away from an Availability Zone during an AWS-detected impairment without waiting for an operator to act. Which feature meets this need?
options: An ARC zonal shift that an operator starts during each event
Route 53 weighted records that split traffic across the zones
ARC zonal autoshift enabled for the load balancer resource
Cross-zone load balancing turned off on the load balancer
questions.correct_rationale: With zonal autoshift, the customer authorizes AWS to shift resource traffic away from an Availability Zone during events, on their behalf. A zonal shift does the same move but is started by an operator.
distractor_rationales: A zonal shift moves traffic away from a zone, but an operator has to start it each time.
Weighted records split traffic by fixed weights and do not react to zone impairments by themselves.
Turning off cross-zone load balancing changes how traffic is spread; it does not move traffic away from an impaired zone.
questions.distractor_summary: Hands-off traffic movement during AWS-detected events is zonal autoshift; a zonal shift needs an operator.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Implement highly available and resilient environments.
questions.question: A node-based ElastiCache cluster has one primary node and one replica, both in the same Availability Zone. The team wants the cache to keep accepting writes if that zone fails, without changing the endpoint the application uses. Which configuration is recommended?
options: A larger node type for the primary, kept in the same Availability Zone
Daily backups of the cluster that are restored after a failure
Multi-AZ with automatic failover, with the replica in another Availability Zone
A second cluster in another zone that the application writes to as well
questions.correct_rationale: Multi-AZ is the recommended configuration for high availability in ElastiCache. When the primary fails, a replica in another zone is promoted and the primary endpoint's DNS name follows it, so the application keeps writing to the same endpoint.
distractor_rationales: A larger node in the same zone still fails with that zone.
Restoring a backup takes time and creates a new cluster with a new endpoint.
A second cluster means the application writes to two endpoints and handles failover itself.
questions.distractor_summary: Surviving a zone failure on the same endpoint is Multi-AZ with automatic failover.

docLinks.title: Minimizing downtime in ElastiCache by using Multi-AZ with Valkey and Redis OSS - Amazon ElastiCache

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Implement backup and restore strategies.
questions.question: An orders table in DynamoDB must be restorable to any second within the last 35 days if a bad deployment corrupts items. The application must also keep reading and writing locally in a second Region if the primary Region becomes unavailable. Which configuration meets both needs?
options: Point-in-time recovery, with no replica in the second Region
Point-in-time recovery, plus a global table replica in the second Region
A global table replica in the second Region, with point-in-time recovery turned off
A weekly on-demand backup kept in the same Region, with no second-Region replica
questions.correct_rationale: Point-in-time recovery provides up to 35 days of recovery points at per-second granularity, which covers restoring before a bad deployment. Global tables replicate the table across Regions with local reads and writes in each, which covers losing the primary Region.
distractor_rationales: Point-in-time recovery restores any second, but nothing serves reads and writes in the second Region.
The replica keeps the application running in the second Region, but replication copies corrupt items too and there is no per-second restore.
A weekly backup cannot restore to any second, and nothing runs in a second Region.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-second restore needs point-in-time recovery and second-Region writes need a global table; each simpler setup drops one.

docLinks.title: Point-in-time backups for DynamoDB - Amazon DynamoDB

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Implement backup and restore strategies.
questions.question: Users of an S3 bucket sometimes overwrite or delete reports by mistake, and the team must be able to restore earlier copies. Storage use must not grow without limit, so earlier copies should be removed 30 days after they are replaced. Which configuration meets these needs?
options: S3 Versioning, plus a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after 30 days
S3 Versioning, plus a lifecycle rule that expires the current object versions after 30 days
A lifecycle rule that expires objects after 30 days, with versioning left off
Cross-Region Replication to a second bucket, with versioning left off
questions.correct_rationale: S3 Versioning preserves every version of every object, so overwritten or deleted reports can be restored. A lifecycle rule with a noncurrent-version expiration removes earlier versions a set number of days after they stop being current.
distractor_rationales: Expiring current versions deletes the live reports after 30 days instead of the replaced copies.
Without versioning, an overwrite or delete leaves no earlier copy to restore.
Replication cannot be configured without versioning, and it does not limit how long earlier copies are kept.
questions.distractor_summary: Restore needs versioning and the 30-day cleanup needs noncurrent-version expiration; the others delete live data or keep no history.

docLinks.title: Retaining multiple versions of objects with S3 Versioning - Amazon Simple Storage Service
Examples of S3 Lifecycle configurations - Amazon Simple Storage Service

questions.subdomain: 2.3 Implement backup and restore strategies.
questions.question: A company runs an Aurora MySQL cluster in one Region. For disaster recovery, it needs a copy of the database in another Region that is kept up to date with replication lag typically under a second and that can take over as the writer if the primary Region fails. Which approach meets this need?
options: Daily Aurora snapshots copied to the recovery Region
An Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in another Region
An Aurora Replica in another Availability Zone of the same primary Region
AWS Backup cross-Region copies of the cluster made every hour
questions.correct_rationale: An Aurora global database has a primary cluster in one Region and secondary clusters in other Regions, replicated with latency typically under a second. A secondary cluster can be promoted through switchover or failover.
distractor_rationales: Daily snapshots can lose up to a day of data and must be restored before use.
A replica in the same Region does not survive the loss of that Region.
Hourly backup copies can lose up to an hour of data and must be restored before use.
questions.distractor_summary: Sub-second cross-Region replication with a promotable copy is an Aurora global database.

docLinks.title: Using Amazon Aurora Global Database - Amazon Aurora

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Provision and maintain cloud resources.
questions.question: An ECS service uses rolling deployments. A deployment must roll back automatically if its new tasks cannot reach a steady state. A deployment must also be marked failed when a CloudWatch alarm on the service's HTTP 5xx rate goes into ALARM, even when the tasks themselves are running. Which configuration meets both needs?
options: The deployment circuit breaker with rollback, and no alarm-based failure detection
Alarm-based deployment failure detection on the 5xx alarm, and no circuit breaker
The deployment circuit breaker with rollback, plus CloudWatch alarm-based deployment failure detection
A higher minimum healthy percent, with no circuit breaker and no alarm detection
questions.correct_rationale: The deployment circuit breaker watches whether tasks reach a steady state and can roll a failed deployment back to the last COMPLETED one. Alarm-based detection sets the deployment to failed when a chosen CloudWatch alarm goes into ALARM, which catches errors in tasks that are running.
distractor_rationales: The circuit breaker handles tasks that never stabilize, but a running deployment with a high 5xx rate is not marked failed.
The alarm catches the 5xx rate, but tasks that never reach a steady state are not rolled back by the breaker.
A higher minimum healthy percent keeps more old tasks during the rollout but detects nothing.
questions.distractor_summary: Steady-state rollback needs the circuit breaker and the 5xx rule needs alarm-based detection; each simpler setup drops one.

docLinks.title: How the Amazon ECS deployment circuit breaker detects failures - Amazon Elastic Container Service
How CloudWatch alarms detect Amazon ECS deployment failures - Amazon Elastic Container Service

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Provision and maintain cloud resources.
questions.question: A platform team publishes golden AMIs. The current golden AMI must not be deregistrable by any user, regardless of their IAM permissions. The previous golden AMI must be marked as out of date from the first day of next month so that teams stop selecting it. Which actions meet both needs?
options: Turn on deregistration protection for the current AMI and set the previous AMI's deprecation date
Turn on deregistration protection for the current AMI, and leave the previous AMI as it is
Set the previous AMI's deprecation date, and leave the current AMI as it is
Copy both AMIs to a second Region as backups, and leave each AMI's settings unchanged
questions.correct_rationale: With deregistration protection on, an AMI cannot be deregistered by any user, regardless of IAM permissions. Deprecating an AMI marks it as out of date, and a future deprecation date sets when that happens.
distractor_rationales: The current AMI is protected, but the previous one is never marked out of date.
The previous AMI gets its deprecation date, but the current AMI can still be deregistered.
Copies in another Region neither protect the current AMI nor mark the previous one.
questions.distractor_summary: Protection needs deregistration protection and the date needs a deprecation setting; each simpler action does one.

docLinks.title: Protect an Amazon EC2 AMI from deregistration - Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud
Deprecate an Amazon EC2 AMI - Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Provision and maintain cloud resources.
questions.question: Several engineers run Terraform against the same AWS environment, and its state is stored with the S3 backend. Twice, two engineers ran apply at the same time and corrupted the state. Which change prevents concurrent runs from writing the same state?
options: Enable state locking in the S3 backend by setting use_lockfile to true
Turn on S3 Versioning for the state bucket and restore after each conflict
Keep a separate local state file on each engineer's own workstation
Add a bucket policy that denies deletes of the state file object
questions.correct_rationale: The S3 backend supports state locking, turned on by setting use_lockfile to true. With a lock held, a second apply waits or fails instead of writing the same state at the same time.
distractor_rationales: Versioning helps recover after corruption but does not stop two runs from writing at once.
Separate local states mean each engineer works from a different view of the environment, which causes drift.
Denying deletes does not stop two runs from overwriting the state.
questions.distractor_summary: Concurrent writes are prevented by state locking; the others only recover, split, or protect against deletes.

docLinks.title: Backend Type: s3 | Terraform | HashiCorp Developer

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Provision and maintain cloud resources.
questions.question: Developers deploy CloudFormation stacks, but the security team does not want developers to hold permissions to create the stacks' resources directly. A CloudFormation service role with those permissions exists. When a developer specifies the role on a stack, the operation fails with an access denied error for the role. Which permission must the developer be given?
options: iam:CreateRole for new roles in the account
sts:AssumeRole on the developer's own IAM user
cloudformation:CreateStackSet on the management account
iam:PassRole on the CloudFormation service role
questions.correct_rationale: A CloudFormation service role lets CloudFormation call the stack's resources on the developer's behalf. Handing a role to a service is passing the role, which needs iam:PassRole on that role.
distractor_rationales: Creating roles is not needed; the role already exists, and the failure is about passing it.
AssumeRole applies to roles, not to a user, and the developer does not assume the service role.
StackSets are unrelated to passing a service role for a single stack.
questions.distractor_summary: Using an existing service role requires iam:PassRole on it.

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Provision and maintain cloud resources.
questions.question: A team has published version 8 of a Lambda function. Clients invoke the function through an alias named live that points to version 7. The team wants 10 percent of invocations to go to version 8 while it watches error metrics. What should the team do?
options: Point clients at version 8 directly for 10 percent of each day
Configure the live alias to route 10 percent of traffic to version 8
Set reserved concurrency on version 8 to 10 percent of the account limit
Publish version 8 under a new alias and update 10 percent of the clients
questions.correct_rationale: A weighted alias splits traffic between two versions of the same function, so the live alias can send 10 percent to version 8 without any client change.
distractor_rationales: Switching by time of day is not a percentage split and needs client changes.
Reserved concurrency caps concurrent executions; it does not route a share of traffic.
Updating a tenth of the clients is slow and does not give an even percentage split.
questions.distractor_summary: A weighted alias splits invocations between versions without touching clients.

docLinks.title: Implement Lambda canary deployments using a weighted alias - AWS Lambda

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Provision and maintain cloud resources.
questions.question: An Elastic Beanstalk environment must keep full capacity during application deployments, and a failed deployment must be undone quickly without performing another rolling update. Which deployment policy meets these needs?
options: Rolling, which updates existing instances one batch at a time
All at once, which updates every existing instance at the same time
Immutable, which launches new instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group
Rolling with additional batch, which adds a batch and then updates in place
questions.correct_rationale: An immutable update launches the new version on new instances in a second, temporary Auto Scaling group behind the load balancer, so existing capacity keeps serving. If it fails, rollback only requires terminating that group.
distractor_rationales: Rolling takes batches out of service, so capacity drops, and undoing it needs another rolling update.
All at once replaces the version on every instance together, risking an outage and offering no quick rollback.
Rolling with additional batch keeps capacity, but undoing a failure still needs another rolling update.
questions.distractor_summary: Full capacity plus a quick rollback by terminating a group is the immutable policy.

docLinks.title: Immutable environment updates - AWS Elastic Beanstalk
Deployment policies and settings - AWS Elastic Beanstalk

questions.subdomain: 3.1 Provision and maintain cloud resources.
questions.question: New Pods on an EKS cluster stay pending, and the Amazon VPC CNI reports that it cannot assign IP addresses. The nodes' primary network interfaces are in small subnets that are almost full, and the VPC has a secondary CIDR block with large unused subnets. Which change lets Pods get addresses without moving the nodes?
options: Add more worker nodes to the same small subnets in each Availability Zone of the cluster
Turn on CNI custom networking so that Pod interfaces use the larger subnets
Raise each Pod's CPU requests so that fewer Pods run on each node
Replace the cluster security groups with groups that allow all traffic
questions.correct_rationale: Pods get addresses from the subnet of the node's primary interface, which has a limited number of IPv4 addresses. Custom networking places the secondary interfaces, and so the Pods, in different subnets such as those in the secondary CIDR block.
distractor_rationales: More nodes in the same subnets consume even more of the scarce addresses.
Fewer Pods per node hides the symptom and still cannot schedule the new Pods.
Security groups control traffic; they do not supply IP addresses.
questions.distractor_summary: Address exhaustion in node subnets is solved by moving Pod interfaces to other subnets with custom networking.

docLinks.title: Deploy Pods in alternate subnets with custom networking - Amazon EKS

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Automate the management of existing resources.
questions.question: A Step Functions state machine calls a partner API from a Task state. Transient timeouts from the API must be retried automatically with increasing waits between attempts. If the call still fails, the execution must move to a state that notifies the operations team instead of simply failing. Which configuration meets both needs?
options: A Retry field with backoff, and a Catch field to the notify state
A Retry field with backoff on the Task state, and no Catch field
A Catch field to the notify state, and no Retry field on the state
Neither field, with the operations team rerunning failed executions by hand
questions.correct_rationale: Step Functions state machines can retry failed states and catch errors. A Retry field with a backoff rate handles transient timeouts with growing waits, and a Catch field sends the execution to the notify state when the errors persist.
distractor_rationales: Retries handle transient timeouts, but a persistent failure still ends the execution without notifying anyone.
The Catch field notifies the team, but transient timeouts are not retried.
Rerunning by hand neither retries automatically nor notifies the team.
questions.distractor_summary: Automatic retries need a Retry field and the notify path needs a Catch field; each simpler setup drops one.

docLinks.title: Handling errors in Step Functions workflows - AWS Step Functions

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Automate the management of existing resources.
questions.question: An administrator adds an S3 event notification that should publish to an existing Amazon SNS topic whenever an object is created. Saving the configuration fails because S3 cannot validate the destination. What should the administrator change?
options: Turn on S3 Versioning so that every new object creates a numbered version
Attach a policy to the administrator's IAM user that allows sns:Subscribe
Encrypt the bucket with SSE-S3 so that each new object is encrypted by default at rest
Add a topic access policy statement that lets the S3 service principal publish
questions.correct_rationale: S3 must be granted permission to publish to the destination SNS topic, SQS queue, or Lambda function. Without a topic policy statement for the S3 service principal, S3 cannot validate the destination.
distractor_rationales: Versioning does not affect whether S3 may publish to the topic.
Subscribe permission for the administrator does not let S3 publish.
Default encryption does not grant S3 permission to publish to the topic.
questions.distractor_summary: S3 needs permission on the destination topic; the other changes do not grant it.

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Automate the management of existing resources.
questions.question: A Lambda function processes batches of 10 messages from an SQS queue. When one message in a batch fails, only that message must be retried, not the messages that were processed successfully. A message that keeps failing must be moved aside after five receives so that it stops blocking work. Which configuration meets both needs?
options: Partial batch responses in the event source mapping, and no dead-letter queue
Partial batch responses in the event source mapping, plus a dead-letter queue with maxReceiveCount 5
A dead-letter queue on the source queue with maxReceiveCount 5, and no partial batch responses
A longer visibility timeout, with no partial batch responses or dead-letter queue
questions.correct_rationale: With partial batch responses, the function reports only the failed messages, so successful ones are not retried. A redrive policy with maxReceiveCount moves a message to a dead-letter queue after that many receives.
distractor_rationales: Only failed messages are retried, but a message that always fails keeps coming back.
Repeat failures are moved aside, but one failure still makes the whole batch retry.
A longer timeout delays retries but changes neither behavior.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-message retries need partial batch responses and moving repeat failures needs a dead-letter queue; each simpler setup drops one.

docLinks.title: Handling errors for an SQS event source in Lambda - AWS Lambda

questions.subdomain: 3.2 Automate the management of existing resources.
questions.question: An EventBridge rule invokes a remediation Lambda function asynchronously. Events that fail every retry must be kept for reprocessing, and each stored record must include details of the function's error response as well as the event. Which configuration meets this need?
options: An on-failure destination in the function's asynchronous invocation settings
A dead-letter queue on the function that receives the discarded events
An on-success destination in the function's asynchronous invocation configuration
Reserved concurrency on the function so that more invocations can run
questions.correct_rationale: Destinations for asynchronous invocations receive records with details about the request and the response, and an on-failure destination receives events that fail all processing attempts. A dead-letter queue receives only the content of the event.
distractor_rationales: A dead-letter queue keeps the event but not the error response details.
An on-success destination records successful events, not failed ones.
Reserved concurrency changes capacity; it keeps no record of failed events.
questions.distractor_summary: Keeping failed events with response details is an on-failure destination; a dead-letter queue keeps only the event.

docLinks.title: Capturing records of Lambda asynchronous invocations - AWS Lambda

questions.question: An order service publishes every order to one SNS topic. The EU fulfillment queue is subscribed to the topic but should receive just the orders whose region message attribute is EU. What is the simplest way to achieve this?

questions.question: An Application Load Balancer target group checks the path / on each instance, and that page loads even when the application cannot reach its database. Health check path changed to /healthz, and deregistration delay left at its 30 seconds

The new ALB gets its share, but us-east-1 keeps receiving new connections during maintenance.
Nothing changes: us-east-1 keeps its traffic and the new ALB gets none.

Retention changed to a count of 4, and AMI deprecation turned on with a count of 2
Age retention of 1 year kept, and AMI deprecation turned on after 14 days

After that, the workflow must pause until a release manager clicks an approval link in an email, which can take anywhere from minutes to days. Which task design meets both needs?

A Batch task using Request Response, then a task using .waitForTaskToken for the approval

The approval pause works, but Request Response moves on as soon as the job is submitted.
The workflow moves on before the job ends, and a fixed wait ignores the approval.

questions.question: A nightly job must process 2 million S3 objects listed in a CSV manifest, running many items in parallel, with each item's processing history kept separate so a failed item can be inspected. A few bad objects are normal, but the whole run must fail if more than 5 percent of items fail. Which design meets both needs?

A Lambda function that loops over the CSV and stops after 5 percent of items fail
A Lambda function that loops over the CSV and stops at the first failed item
A Distributed Map reading the CSV, with ToleratedFailurePercentage set to 5

The 5 percent rule is coded, but one function loops serially with no per-item history, and 2 million objects will not finish within its time limit.
A single looping function lacks parallelism and per-item history, and it stops at the first bad object.

One-time schedules kept in UTC as today, with deletion after completion turned on
One-time schedules in America/New_York, with deletion after completion turned on
One-time schedules kept in UTC, with no action after completion, both as today

Finished schedules are cleaned up, but 14:00 UTC is 9:00 AM in New York for only part of the year.
Reminders drift by an hour when daylight saving changes, and finished schedules pile up.

questions.question: A Step Functions task sends a task token to an on-premises worker and waits for the callback. The worker sends a heartbeat every few minutes while it works, and if 10 minutes pass with no heartbeat the task must fail so a Catch can alert the team. Separately, the task must fail if the work is not finished within 8 hours, even while heartbeats keep arriving. Which Task state settings meet both needs?
options: HeartbeatSeconds of 600, and TimeoutSeconds left unset on the task
HeartbeatSeconds of 600, and TimeoutSeconds of 28800 on the task
HeartbeatSeconds left unset, and TimeoutSeconds of 28800 on the task
HeartbeatSeconds and TimeoutSeconds both left unset, with a Retry

The 8-hour limit is set, but a worker that stops sending heartbeats is not caught until 8 hours pass.
Neither failure is detected, and a Retry does nothing when no timeout fires.

questions.question: A deployment pipeline updates IAM policies. It must fail a change when the updated policy grants any access that the current version does not. It must also fail any policy that allows iam:PassRole, whatever the current version contains. Which IAM Access Analyzer checks meet both needs with the least pipeline work?

CheckNoNewAccess against the current version, which would also flag an iam:PassRole that it adds
CheckAccessNotGranted for iam:PassRole, run on its own against the updated policy
Policy validation findings on the updated policy, treating any warning as a failure

PassRole is blocked, but CheckAccessNotGranted does not compare the update with the current version, so other new access passes.
Policy validation reports grammar and best-practice findings; it neither compares versions nor tests for iam:PassRole.

The bucket must now accept requests from principals in any account of the company's organization, including accounts added later, and from no one outside it. Every request must also arrive over TLS. Keep that statement as it is, and add a Deny statement for aws:SecureTransport false
Change that statement to test aws:PrincipalOrgID, and add a Deny for aws:SecureTransport false

TLS is enforced, but the account condition still denies every other account in the organization.
Other organization accounts are still denied, and an encryption header governs encryption at rest, not TLS.

lessons.domain: 1. Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
lessons.title: Alarm on the right signal, then let AWS fix it
body: Start by checking that the metric exists. EC2 publishes its standard metrics by default, but memory and disk usage inside the operating system come from the CloudWatch agent, which collects in-guest system-level metrics. No metric means no alarm.

Next, cut the noise. A metric alarm watches one metric or expression against a threshold. When one failure trips several alarms, create a composite alarm whose rule references them, for example ALARM only when every child is in ALARM, and send alerts only from the composite. Composite alarms can notify SNS and create OpsItems or incidents, but they cannot perform EC2 or Auto Scaling actions, so keep those on metric alarms.

Then automate the response. AWS Config remediates noncompliant resources with Systems Manager Automation documents; managed documents exist, and you can write custom ones. Automation also ships predefined runbooks for common tasks such as restarting EC2 instances. Finally, tune the resource itself: gp3 volumes scale IOPS and throughput independently of size and do not burst, and RDS Proxy pools database connections so that bursts of short-lived clients stop exhausting the instance.

lessons.title: Trace the packet: routes, filters, endpoints, edge
body: When a connection fails, follow its path in order. First the route: does the subnet route table send the traffic where you expect? A gateway endpoint for S3 or DynamoDB adds a prefix-list route to the route tables you select, and it has no additional charge, so it is the usual fix for NAT gateway charges on S3 traffic from the same Region.

Next the filters. Security groups are stateful: responses to allowed requests return automatically. Network ACLs are stateless and are evaluated as traffic enters and leaves the subnet, so an inbound allow does not cover the response; the outbound rules must allow it too. VPC Flow Logs capture information about IP traffic to and from network interfaces and help show where traffic stops.

Then the boundary. Gateway endpoints do not accept traffic from on-premises networks, peered VPCs in other Regions or a transit gateway; those paths need an interface endpoint, at extra cost. For outbound-only IPv6, use an egress-only internet gateway; for IPv4, a NAT gateway. At the edge, CloudFront caches content close to users, while Global Accelerator gives static anycast IP addresses in front of load balancers in one or more Regions.
decisions: Private subnets send heavy S3 traffic through NAT
